title: JavaScript Fundamentals
tagline: Before Thursday. The multiple-choice favourites: scope, closures, this, coercion.

topics.title: Types, equality and coercion
topics.summary: Predict what weird expressions return.
items: 7 primitives (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null) vs objects
typeof null === 'object', typeof [] === 'object', typeof function(){} === 'function'
== coerces, === does not; always use === except `x == null`
Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN (everything else is truthy, including [] and {})
NaN !== NaN; use Number.isNaN
0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 (floating point); compare with a tolerance
Objects compare by reference: {} === {} is false

questions.q: What does [] + {} return? And [] == false?
questions.a:
- `[] + {}` → "[object Object]". Both become strings: "" + "[object Object]".
- `[] == false` → true. [] → "" → 0, and false → 0.
Lesson: use === to avoid coercion surprises.

questions.q: Difference between null and undefined?
questions.a:
- undefined: a value was never assigned (missing variable value, missing property, function with no return).
- null: deliberately "no value", set by the programmer.
- `typeof undefined` is "undefined", `typeof null` is "object" (a historical bug).
- `null == undefined` is true, `null === undefined` is false. `x == null` checks both at once.

questions.q: How do you deep-copy an object?
questions.a:
`structuredClone(obj)`: built in, handles nested objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets and cycles. It can't copy functions or DOM nodes.
- `{...obj}` / `Object.assign` are shallow: nested objects are still shared.
- `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` is the old trick: loses Dates (become strings), undefined, functions, Maps, and fails on cycles.

concepts.title: Quick quiz with answers
concepts.body:
- `'5' + 3` → "53" (string concatenation wins)
- `'5' - 3` → 2 (minus forces numbers)
- `[] == false` → true ([] → "" → 0, false → 0)
- `null == undefined` → true, `null === undefined` → false
- `null == 0` → false (null only loosely equals undefined)
- `typeof NaN` → "number"
- `[1, 2] + [3]` → "1,23"
- `!!'0'` → true (non-empty string)

topics.title: Scope, hoisting and closures
topics.summary: Where variables live and how long they survive.
items: var is function-scoped and hoisted as undefined
let/const are block-scoped; the temporal dead zone throws before declaration
const prevents reassignment, not mutation
Function declarations are hoisted fully; function expressions are not
A closure is a function plus the variables it captured from where it was created
Use closures for private state, factories, debounce and memoisation

questions.q: What does a for loop with var and setTimeout log? How do you fix it?
questions.a:
```js
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));  // 3 3 3
```
`var` creates one shared `i`; the callbacks run after the loop, when i is 3.
Fix: use `let` (a new binding per iteration) → 0 1 2. Older fix: an IIFE that captures i.

topics.title: this, functions and classes
topics.summary: this depends on how a function is called.
items: Method call obj.f(): this = obj; plain call f(): undefined in strict mode
Arrow functions don't have their own this; they use the surrounding one
call/apply/bind set this explicitly
Prototype chain: objects delegate missing properties to their prototype
class is syntax over prototypes; know constructor, extends, super, static, #private

questions.q: Why does a method lose `this` when passed as a callback? Two ways to fix it
questions.a:
`this` is decided by how a function is called. `button.addEventListener("click", obj.save)` passes the function alone, so when it's called, it's not called as `obj.save()` and `this` is no longer obj.
Fixes:
1. Bind: `obj.save.bind(obj)`
2. Arrow wrapper: `() => obj.save()`
(3. In classes, define the method as an arrow-function field: `save = () => {...}`.)

questions.q: Arrow vs regular function: three differences
questions.a:
1. Arrow functions have no own `this`; they use the surrounding `this`.
2. No `arguments` object (use rest params `...args`).
3. Can't be used as constructors with `new`, and have no `prototype`.
(Also: arrow functions aren't hoisted like function declarations, and can have an implicit return.)

concepts.title: Losing this
concepts.body:
```js
const user = { name: "Ana", hi() { return this.name; } };
const f = user.hi;
f();                    // TypeError/undefined: called without an object
f.call(user);           // "Ana"
const g = user.hi.bind(user); g(); // "Ana"
```
Arrow functions as class fields keep `this` bound to the instance, which is why React class handlers used them.

questions.q: Implement groupBy with reduce
Difference between ?? and ||
questions.a:
- `a || b` returns b if a is any falsy value (0, "", false, null, undefined, NaN).
- `a ?? b` returns b only if a is null or undefined.
So `0 || 10` is 10 but `0 ?? 10` is 0. Use ?? for defaults where 0 or "" are valid values (amounts, counts, empty strings).

questions.q: Why does [10, 1, 2].sort() give [1, 10, 2]?
questions.a: Default sort compares items as strings: "1" < "10" < "2". Use `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)` for numbers.

title: Async JavaScript and the Event Loop
tagline: Before Thursday. Output-order questions are a test favourite.

topics.title: The event loop
topics.summary: Call stack, microtasks, macrotasks: in that order.
items: JS runs one call stack to completion, then drains ALL microtasks, then takes one macrotask
Microtasks: promise callbacks (then/catch/finally), await continuations, queueMicrotask
Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events
setTimeout(fn, 0) still waits for the stack and all microtasks
Rendering happens between macrotasks; long tasks freeze the UI

questions.q: Predict the output order of a snippet mixing console.log, setTimeout and Promise.then
Why doesn't setTimeout(fn, 0) run immediately?
questions.a: It schedules fn as a macrotask. The event loop only runs it after the current synchronous code has finished and every queued microtask (promises) has run. The 0 is a minimum delay, not a guarantee (browsers may clamp it to ~4ms when nested).

concepts.title: Output order

topics.title: Promises and async/await
topics.summary: Write async code that handles failure.
items: Promise states: pending, fulfilled, rejected
Chaining: return values and thrown errors flow down the chain
async functions always return a promise; await unwraps one
try/catch around await; unhandled rejections
Promise.all (fail fast), allSettled, race, any
Run independent requests in parallel, not one after another

questions.q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled: when to use each?
questions.a:
- `Promise.all`: rejects as soon as any promise rejects. Use when you need all results (e.g. user + account to render a page).
- `Promise.allSettled`: waits for all and gives each result as fulfilled/rejected. Use when partial success is fine (e.g. load several dashboard widgets; show errors per widget).
- Also: `Promise.race` (first to settle) for timeouts, `Promise.any` (first to succeed).

questions.q: What is wrong with `await` inside a forEach?
questions.a:
forEach ignores the promise each callback returns, so it doesn't wait. Code after the forEach runs before the work finishes, and errors aren't caught.
```js
for (const id of ids) await save(id);               // one after another
await Promise.all(ids.map((id) => save(id)));       // in parallel
```

title: TypeScript Essentials
tagline: Types that catch bugs without fighting you.

topics.title: Types you use daily
topics.summary: Annotate boundaries, let inference do the rest.
items: type vs interface (interfaces merge and extend; types do unions and more)

unknown over any; never for impossible cases

questions.q: When would you choose type over interface?
questions.a:
- interface: object shapes that may be extended or merged (public APIs, props). Supports `extends` and declaration merging.
- type: anything else, especially unions (`"idle" | "loading"`), intersections, tuples, mapped and conditional types.
Many teams: interface for objects, type for unions. Either is fine for plain props; just be consistent.

questions.q: any vs unknown?
questions.a:
- any: turns off type checking. Anything goes, bugs slip through.
- unknown: you can hold any value but must narrow it before use (typeof, instanceof, a type guard or a schema like zod).
Use unknown for untrusted data (API responses, JSON.parse, catch errors).

title: HTML, CSS and Accessibility
tagline: Layouts you can write by hand, and markup that works for everyone.

topics.title: Semantic HTML and accessibility
topics.summary: Use the right element and most accessibility comes free.
items: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer
button for actions, a for navigation (never a clickable div)
Every input has a label; forms submit with Enter
alt text on images; headings in order
Keyboard: everything reachable with Tab, visible focus, Escape closes modals
ARIA only when no native element exists (aria-label, aria-expanded, role)

questions.q: Why is a div with onClick worse than a button?
questions.a: A `<button>` gives you for free: keyboard focus (Tab), activation with Enter and Space, the "button" role for screen readers, disabled state and form submission. A div has none of that; you'd need tabindex, role, key handlers and focus styles to fake it.

questions.q: How would you make a custom dropdown accessible?
questions.a:
- Prefer a native `<select>` if the design allows.
- Otherwise: a `<button aria-haspopup="listbox" aria-expanded>` that opens a `role="listbox"` with `role="option"` items and `aria-selected`.
- Keyboard: arrows move, Enter/Space selects, Escape closes and returns focus to the button, Home/End.
- Label it, keep visible focus, close on outside click.
Or use a tested library (Radix, Headless UI, React Aria).

topics.title: Box model, flexbox and grid
topics.summary: The live-coding basics.
items: Box model: content, padding, border, margin; box-sizing: border-box
Flexbox: justify-content (main axis), align-items (cross axis), gap, flex: 1
Grid: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))
Center anything: display: grid; place-items: center
Positioning: relative, absolute (to nearest positioned ancestor), fixed, sticky
Margin collapsing between vertical block margins

questions.q: Center a div horizontally and vertically, three ways
Build a responsive card grid without media queries
Flexbox vs grid: when each?
questions.a:
- Flexbox: one dimension (a row or a column). Toolbars, nav bars, aligning items in a line, content-driven sizing.
- Grid: two dimensions (rows and columns together). Page layouts, card grids, dashboards.
They combine well: grid for the page, flex inside components.

topics.title: Cascade, specificity and responsive
topics.summary: Why a style wins, and how pages adapt.
items: Specificity: inline > id > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element
Later rule wins at equal specificity; !important as a last resort
rem vs em vs px vs %; vw/vh; clamp() for fluid type
Mobile-first media queries with min-width

questions.q: Which selector wins: .nav a or #menu a?
questions.a: `#menu a`. An id beats any number of classes. Specificity: (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements) → #menu a = (1,0,1) vs .nav a = (0,1,1).

questions.q: rem vs em?
questions.a:
- rem: relative to the root (html) font size. Predictable; good for spacing and type scales.
- em: relative to the current element's font size, so it compounds when nested. Useful for things that should scale with their own text (button padding, icons).
Both respect the user's browser font-size setting, unlike px.

title: React in Depth
tagline: Before Thursday (basics). State, effects and rendering are guaranteed questions.

topics.title: Components, props and state
topics.summary: UI is a function of state.
items: Props flow down, events flow up via callbacks
useState; updates are async and batched; use the functional form for updates based on the previous value
Never mutate state: create new arrays/objects
Lift state up to the closest common parent
Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs
Derive values during render instead of storing duplicate state

questions.q: Why does setCount(count + 1) twice only add 1?
questions.a:
Both calls read the same `count` from this render (say 0), so both set it to 1. State updates are batched and applied on the next render.
Fix: the functional form uses the latest queued value.
```jsx
setCount((c) => c + 1);
setCount((c) => c + 1);   // now +2
```

questions.q: Controlled vs uncontrolled components?
questions.a:
- Controlled: React state holds the value (`value={x} onChange={e => setX(e.target.value)}`). Easy validation, formatting and conditional UI.
- Uncontrolled: the DOM holds it; read via a ref or FormData on submit (`defaultValue`). Less code, fewer re-renders, good for simple forms.
Libraries like react-hook-form use uncontrolled inputs for performance.

questions.q: When do you lift state up?
questions.a: When two or more sibling components need the same data or need to stay in sync. Move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down as props, with callbacks to change it. If it's needed far away in the tree, consider context or a store.

concepts.title: Updating state correctly
concepts.body:
```jsx
setCount((c) => c + 1);                               // based on previous value
setTodos((ts) => [...ts, newTodo]);                    // add
setTodos((ts) => ts.filter((t) => t.id !== id));       // remove
setTodos((ts) => ts.map((t) => t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)); // update
```

topics.title: Effects and hooks
topics.summary: Effects synchronise with the outside world, nothing else.
items: useEffect runs after render; the dependency array controls when
Cleanup functions: unsubscribe, clear timers, abort fetches
Avoid effects for derived data or event handling
useRef for DOM nodes and mutable values that don't re-render
useMemo / useCallback only for expensive work or stable references
Custom hooks to reuse stateful logic (useDebounce, useFetch)
Rules of hooks: top level only, only in components or hooks

questions.q: What happens with a missing dependency? An object as a dependency?
questions.a:
- Missing dependency: the effect keeps using a stale value from an old render (stale closure) and doesn't re-run when it changes. Bugs that are hard to spot. The eslint rule `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` catches it.
- Object/array/function created during render: it's a new reference every render, so the effect runs every time (maybe in a loop if it sets state). Fix: depend on primitive fields, create it inside the effect, or memoise with useMemo/useCallback.

questions.q: Why does an effect run twice in development (Strict Mode)?
questions.a: React 18+ Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and remounts components in development to expose effects without proper cleanup. It doesn't happen in production. The fix is to write effects whose cleanup undoes the setup (unsubscribe, abort fetch, clear timers), not to remove Strict Mode.

topics.title: Rendering and performance
topics.summary: Know why a component re-renders.
items: Re-render triggers: own state change, parent re-render, context change
Keys: stable ids, not array indexes for reorderable lists
React.memo + stable props to skip re-renders
Context re-renders all consumers; split contexts
Lazy loading with React.lazy and Suspense; code splitting
Virtualise long lists

questions.q: Why are index keys a problem?
questions.a: Keys tell React which item is which between renders. With index keys, inserting, deleting or reordering items shifts the indexes, so React reuses the wrong component: state (like input text or checkboxes) ends up on the wrong row, and more DOM work is done. Use a stable unique id. Index is fine only for static lists that never change order.

questions.q: A list of 10,000 rows is slow. What do you check?
questions.a:
1. Profile first (React DevTools Profiler, Performance tab).
2. Virtualise: only render visible rows (TanStack Virtual, react-window).
3. Stable keys; memoise rows (React.memo) and pass stable props/callbacks.
4. Avoid heavy work in render: precompute or useMemo for filtering/sorting.
5. Paginate or load more from the server instead of sending 10,000 rows.
6. Debounce filter inputs; consider useDeferredValue.

topics.title: Next.js and the ecosystem
topics.summary: What you already use, explained clearly.
items: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR, and why SSR helps SEO (your CRSTRIP Nuxt work)
Server Components vs Client Components in the Next.js App Router
Routing, layouts and loading states
State: local state, context, Zustand/Redux, server cache (TanStack Query)
Forms and validation (react-hook-form + zod)

questions.q: SSR vs CSR trade-offs?
questions.a:
- SSR: HTML is rendered on the server, so first content appears fast and it's SEO-friendly (search engines see full HTML). Costs server work, needs hydration, and some code must run in both environments.
- CSR: the server sends a JS app that renders in the browser. Simple hosting, rich interactivity after load, but a slower first paint and weaker SEO.
- SSG/ISR: pre-render at build time / periodically; fastest for content that doesn't change per user.
Example from CRSTRIP: Nuxt SSR for SEO on booking pages plus runtime theme switching per domain.

questions.q: Where should server data live in a React app?
questions.a: In a server-state cache like TanStack Query or SWR (or the framework's loaders / Server Components), not copied into useState or Redux. They handle caching, deduping, refetching, loading and error states and invalidation after mutations. Keep useState/context for UI state (open modals, form inputs, theme).

title: The Browser, Performance and Security
tagline: How the page actually works, and what a bank cares about.

topics.title: DOM and events
topics.summary: Bubbling, delegation, and not leaking listeners.
items: Event phases: capture, target, bubble; stopPropagation vs preventDefault
Event delegation: one listener on a parent, check event.target
Remove listeners and observers on cleanup
IntersectionObserver for lazy loading and infinite scroll

questions.q: What is event delegation and why use it?
preventDefault vs stopPropagation?
questions.a:
- preventDefault: stops the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form, checking a box). The event still bubbles.
- stopPropagation: stops the event bubbling to parent elements. The default action still happens.
They're independent; use only what you need (stopPropagation can break delegation and analytics).

topics.title: Rendering and performance
topics.summary: Fast first load, smooth interaction.
items: Critical rendering path: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, layout, paint, composite
Core Web Vitals: LCP (load), INP (responsiveness), CLS (layout shift)
Reduce bundle size: code splitting, tree shaking, analyse the bundle (your 32% at HARA AI)
Images: modern formats, sizes, lazy loading; fonts: font-display
Caching: HTTP cache headers, CDN, service workers
Debounce/throttle expensive handlers

questions.q: How did you cut the bundle by 32%?
questions.a:
Prepare your real answer. A strong structure:
- Measured first: bundle analyser to find the biggest modules.
- Changes, e.g.: code-split routes and heavy components with dynamic import; replaced or tree-shook large libraries (only importing what's used, lighter date/icon libs); removed dead code and duplicate dependencies; upgraded React/Next/MUI.
- Result: 32% smaller bundle, faster page loads.
Only say what you actually did, and be ready for "how did you measure it?".

questions.q: A page feels slow. Walk me through how you'd investigate
questions.a:
1. Reproduce and measure: Lighthouse / Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), on a throttled connection and a slow device.
2. Network tab: big bundles, slow API calls, waterfalls, uncompressed or uncached assets, huge images.
3. Performance tab: long tasks on the main thread, layout thrashing, expensive re-renders (React Profiler).
4. Fix the biggest issue first: code splitting, caching, image optimisation, parallel requests, memoisation or virtualisation.
5. Measure again to confirm.

topics.title: Web security
topics.summary: Fintech interviewers love this.
items: XSS: never inject untrusted HTML; React escapes by default; beware dangerouslySetInnerHTML
CSRF: SameSite cookies and tokens
CORS is enforced by the browser for cross-origin reads; it is not authentication
Store tokens in httpOnly cookies rather than localStorage when possible
Content Security Policy; HTTPS everywhere

questions.q: Where would you store an auth token and why?
questions.a:
Prefer an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie set by the server: JavaScript can't read it, so an XSS bug can't steal it. Add CSRF protection (SameSite plus a CSRF token for state-changing requests).
localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so any XSS leaks the token. If you must keep a token in JS, keep a short-lived access token in memory and refresh via an httpOnly cookie.

questions.q: What is XSS and how does React help?
questions.a:
Cross-site scripting: an attacker gets their script to run in your page (e.g. via a comment containing `<script>`), and it can steal data or act as the user.
React escapes values rendered in JSX by default, so text is shown as text, not run as HTML. Risks remain with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (sanitise with DOMPurify), `href={userInput}` (block `javascript:` URLs), and third-party scripts. Add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

topics.title: Storage and networking
topics.summary: Where data lives in the browser.
items: localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies vs IndexedDB
HTTP methods, status codes, idempotency
REST vs GraphQL basics; WebSockets / SSE for live data

questions.q: How would you show live balance updates?
questions.a:
- Server pushes changes: WebSockets (two-way) or Server-Sent Events (server → client, simpler, auto-reconnect).
- On each event, update the cached balance (e.g. TanStack Query `setQueryData`), so the UI re-renders.
- Handle reconnects and gaps: on reconnect, refetch the latest balance from the API (the source of truth).
- Fallback: polling every few seconds if sockets aren't available.
- For money: never trust only the client value; show pending states for transactions in flight.

topics.title: Unit tests with Vitest/Jest
topics.summary: Arrange, Act, Assert. One behaviour per test.
items: describe / it / expect; toBe vs toEqual
Test the normal case, edge cases and the failure case
Name tests as behaviour: 'returns 0 for an empty list'
Test pure functions first; they are easiest

questions.q: What would you test for a formatCurrency(amount, currency) function?
questions.a:
- Normal: 1234.5 GBP → "£1,234.50"
- Zero and negatives: 0 → "£0.00", -5 → "-£5.00"
- Rounding: 1.005, 0.1 + 0.2
- Large numbers and separators: 1,000,000
- Different currencies and decimals: EUR, USD, JPY (no decimals)
- Locale if supported
- Invalid input: NaN, Infinity, undefined, unknown currency code → throws or a defined fallback
Mention: store money in minor units (pence) as integers to avoid float errors.

questions.q: toBe vs toEqual?
questions.a: `toBe` checks identity with Object.is, right for primitives (numbers, strings, booleans). `toEqual` compares structure recursively, needed for objects and arrays (`expect({a: 1}).toEqual({a: 1})` passes, `toBe` fails). `toStrictEqual` also checks undefined properties and class types.

questions.q: How would you test a login form?
questions.a:
With Testing Library, from the user's point of view (mock the API with MSW or a mocked function):
- Renders email and password fields with labels and a submit button
- Shows validation errors for an empty or invalid email, without calling the API
- Submits the right data and shows a loading state (button disabled)
- On success: redirects or shows the logged-in state
- On a 401: shows "wrong email or password" and keeps the email filled in
- On a network error: shows a retry message
- Accessibility: submit with Enter; errors linked to fields

questions.q: getBy vs queryBy vs findBy?
questions.a:
- getBy: element must exist now; throws if missing. Default choice.
- queryBy: returns null if missing; use to assert something is NOT there (`expect(queryByText("Error")).toBeNull()`).
- findBy: async; waits until the element appears (returns a promise). Use after fetches or timers.
Each has an *AllBy* version for multiple elements.

E2E with Playwright or Cypress for critical flows (login, payment)
Defensive code: validate input, handle errors, show fallback UI
Error boundaries in React

questions.q: What would you test first in a payments screen?
questions.a:
The flows where a bug costs money or trust:
1. Correct amount and currency shown and sent (formatting, rounding, minor units)
2. Validation: insufficient balance, invalid amount, zero/negative, limits
3. No double submission (button disabled while pending; idempotency key)
4. Error states: network failure, declined payment, timeout, with a clear message and no lost input
5. Success state and the balance/transactions updating
Plus one end-to-end test of the happy path.

questions.q: How do you decide what NOT to test?
questions.a: Skip tests that only re-check the framework or third-party code, trivial getters and pure markup, and implementation details (internal state, private functions) that make tests break on harmless refactors. Focus on behaviour users rely on, business rules, edge cases and things that have broken before. Aim for confidence per test, not a coverage number.

mustKnow: Normal, edge and failure cases for any function

concepts.title: How to talk while coding
concepts.body:
1. Restate the task and ask 1-2 clarifying questions (empty state? mobile?)
2. Say the plan: components, state, data flow
3. Build the simplest working version first
4. Then add edge cases: empty, loading, error, very long text
5. Mention what you would add with more time: tests, accessibility, performance
Forgot an API? Say: "I'd check MDN for the exact signature, but it's roughly..." and keep going.

questions.q: Design a transaction history screen for a banking app
questions.a:
Structure your answer:
1. Requirements: list grouped by day, search and filters (category, date, amount), details view, pending vs completed, multiple currencies.
2. Data: paginated API with a cursor; infinite scroll; TanStack Query for caching and refetch; optimistic updates are rare here (read-heavy).
3. Components: TransactionList (virtualised) → DayGroup → TransactionRow; FilterBar; TransactionDetail drawer/page.
4. State: filters in the URL (shareable, back button works); server data in the query cache.
5. UX states: loading skeletons, empty, error with retry, offline banner, pending badges.
6. Performance: virtualisation, image/icon caching, prefetch the next page.
7. Accessibility and i18n: screen-reader labels for amounts ("minus 20 pounds"), date/currency formatting with Intl.
8. Security: no sensitive data in logs/URLs, auto-logout.

questions.q: Design an autocomplete component
questions.a:
- Input with debounce (~300ms); cancel stale requests with AbortController so old results can't overwrite new ones.
- Cache results per query; minimum characters before searching.
- Keyboard: up/down to move, Enter to select, Escape to close; highlight the matching text.
- Accessibility: combobox pattern (`role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `aria-activedescendant`, a `listbox` of `option`s).
- States: loading, no results, error.
- Performance: limit results, virtualise if long.
- API: `<Autocomplete fetchOptions onSelect renderOption />`.

questions.q: Tell me about a technical challenge you're proud of
questions.a:
Use STAR, about 90 seconds. Nobatix double booking is a strong choice:
- Situation: online booking platform for clinics and salons in beta.
- Task: two customers must never book the same slot.
- Action: first DB transactions with checks in app logic; as load grew, added Redis to coordinate slot reservations, with the DB staying the source of truth; designed appointments as snapshots plus nullable external IDs.
- Result: correct under concurrency, scalable, and history stays accurate.
Link: "same problem as making sure money can't be spent twice."

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked under pressure
questions.a:
Use STAR with a real example. Options:
- Getting Simorgh's proposals, website and referral materials ready while studying full-time on an MSc.
- A deadline at CRSTRIP delivering white-label booking sites for several clients from one codebase.
Show: how you prioritised (what mattered most), how you communicated with the team, what you delivered, and one thing you'd do differently. Keep it calm and concrete.

questions.q: Why Revolut, and why frontend?
questions.a:
- Why Revolut: scale (tens of millions of customers, so the work matters), a culture of speed and ownership that matches how you've worked in your own company, and a strong graduate programme with mentorship.
- Why frontend: it's where you have the most production experience (CRSTRIP, HARA AI, Nobatix); you like owning what users actually touch; at a bank, frontend is real engineering (performance, reliability, security, accessibility). Longer term you want to bring AI into products, and great product engineers understand the interface.
